Print the entire `best` table after each outer iteration (i.e., after processing each `value`). Compare the table you obtain with the table you would get if you iterated the inner loop over `coins` in the opposite direction (or iterated `value` descending).
data.trace_question: After the first outer loop (value = 1), what is the value stored in `best[1]`? Does it equal the expected optimal number of coins (1) or the incorrect result (-1) you observed?
data.expected_insight: You will see that `best[1]` remains at its initial large value because the update reads `best[value + coin]` before that entry has been computed. This shows that reading a state before it is written (wrong loop order) leads to the wrong output, contradicting the belief that table order does not matter.
